title: Changing a running system
summary: A safe migration preserves compatibility through the whole rollback window.

steps.title: The new column is ready, but old apps are not
steps.text: You want to replace a free-text address with structured fields. Web code can update today, but mobile clients will keep sending the old shape for months. A migration is a period when multiple schemas and code versions coexist. A deployment that works only after every client updates is not a rollout plan.

steps.title: Expand, move, contract
steps.text: Advance a live table through compatible schema expansion, dual writes, backfill, comparison, cutover and contraction. Inject a stage failure, keep writing, then inspect the rollback boundary.

steps.title: Worked example: how long it takes
steps.text: Retries, live changes, reconciliation, indexes and replicas add work beyond these lower bounds. A canary might admit 1%, 5%, 25% and then all eligible traffic. Percentages do not replace minimum observation time or coverage of large tenants. The traffic engine does not execute schema changes row by row.

diagram.label: Copy time and catch-up time differ
parts: 500 million rows / 5,000 rows/s. About 250 GB at 500 bytes/row.
Include minimum observation time and large-tenant coverage in the canary.

rows.label: Logical copied bytes
rows.how: 500 million × 500 B, before index and replication

steps.q: A backfill reads version 5, then a live write creates version 6. What prevents the delayed copy from regressing the target?
choices: A unique backfill job id used for deduplication
An atomic version check, or snapshot-and-log replay ordered through cutover
A later ingestion timestamp on whichever copy arrives last
steps.why: Deduplication prevents repeated application of one job. Version checks or correctly ordered replay also prevent stale overwrite.

steps.q: Why not write to both databases in the request handler? Follow-up: the first write succeeds and the second times out.
checklist: Treat a timed-out second write as an unknown outcome
Atomically capture source changes and replay versioned target writes
Name one write authority and compare both stores before cutover
steps.model: Two independent writes leave an ambiguous state. I would keep one authority and atomically record its change with an outbox or capture its committed log. The target applies versioned changes idempotently and exposes lag. A timeout is reconciled rather than treated as proof of failure. During cutover I would compare the stores and keep a documented source of truth. A second successful API reply alone does not prove the databases contain the same state.

steps.title: Rollback is a data decision
steps.text: Define which reader versions understand new writes and what happens to writes accepted during a canary. A code rollback is unsafe when old readers cannot understand the new representation. Preserve compatible writes or test a reverse transform. Agree ownership with application and data teams, on-call, security, product and support. Calendar time can be weeks even when copying bytes takes a day.

diagram.label: Rollback follows the data
parts: Keep compatible writes during backfill and the canary.
Mismatch rate, lag, p99 and lock time can pause the rollout.
Dropping old data ends a code-only rollback. Reserve a stable rollback period first.

steps.q: A canary writes a new enum that old code cannot parse. What must be addressed before reverting the binary?
choices: Only restore the old configuration before deploying the old binary
Only stop new canary traffic; its committed data is unaffected by rollback
Preserve old-readable data or test a recovery transform for the new writes
steps.why: New data survives the deployment. Reverting code alone leaves unreadable rows in place.

steps.q: The backfill takes one day. Why did you ask for three weeks? Follow-up: who can stop the rollout?
checklist: Separate copy time from live-write catch-up and verification
Require representative canaries and a tested rollback window
Name the rollout lead and concrete stop thresholds
steps.model: The copy floor excludes throttling, catching live changes, verifying results, representative canaries and a rollback window. Old clients and backup restores may need the old schema longer. I would give application, data and on-call owners shared stop criteria such as mismatch rate, replication lag or p99 regression, with one named rollout lead. For example, stop on any unexplained lost address field, lag beyond the allowed catch-up window, or p99 above the agreed target; choose thresholds from this workload rather than copying them blindly. Product and support need to agree the user states and deprecation deadline. We can shorten the calendar only by explicitly changing that evidence or compatibility requirement.

steps.q: A 1% canary passes for thirty seconds on a low-volume service. What evidence is still missing?
choices: Representative paths and tenants observed long enough to exercise delayed work
A 25% canary for the same thirty seconds, regardless of request mix
A successful deployment health check in every zone
steps.why: More traffic or healthy processes alone can miss rare paths, scheduled jobs and delayed correctness failures.

takeaway: Migrate through compatible states and prove that rollback still understands the data.
